name: Search for Missing Persons (radio program)
description: A 1938 Jack L. Cooper radio program on WSBC dedicated to reuniting Black listeners with family members separated by migration, incarceration, or economic hardship.

name: Dating on the Stroll (47th Street promenade)
description: The evening promenade along State Street and 47th Street — 'the Stroll' — where young Black Chicagoans dressed up, saw and were seen, and courted. Timuel Black: 47th Street was 'the place to gawk and be gawked at.'
notes: Merged into canonical KG 2026-10-03 from LIFE-001; source entity IDs: CTL-DR-LIFE-001:CTL-LIFE-E-011; source research type(s): practice.

name: Family reunions
description: Annual (usually summer) gatherings of extended Black families — born from post-emancipation searches for kin separated by slavery — featuring traditional foods, matching T-shirts, ancestry teaching, and church services or picnics.
notes: Merged into canonical KG 2026-10-03 from LIFE-001; source entity IDs: CTL-DR-LIFE-001:CTL-LIFE-E-014; source research type(s): practice.

name: Soul food cooking in migration-era Chicago
description: Southern culinary traditions carried north in the Great Migration — fried chicken and fish, barbecue, chitterlings, souse, greens, cornbread — first stigmatized by the Black middle class, later embraced as racial identity; adapted to urban kitchens, hot plates, and eventually canned/frozen foods.
notes: Merged into canonical KG 2026-10-03 from LIFE-001; source entity IDs: CTL-DR-LIFE-001:CTL-LIFE-E-023; source research type(s): practice.

name: Hall Branch Library and Vivian Harsh Collection
description: Bronzeville branch of the Chicago Public Library where Vivian G. Harsh — the first African American to run a CPL branch — built a major African American literature/history collection; children's librarian Charlemae Hill-Rollins ran children's programming from 1932 (collection now at Woodson Regional Library).
notes: Merged into canonical KG 2026-10-03 from LIFE-001; source entity IDs: CTL-DR-LIFE-001:CTL-LIFE-E-028; source research type(s): institution.

name: "Don't Spend Your Money Where You Can't Work" boycott pickets on 47th Street
description: Teenagers and adults picketing stores on 47th Street that served Black shoppers but refused to hire Black workers, warning shoppers not to spend money where they couldn't get jobs.

name: Ebony Fashion Fair (Johnson Publishing Company)
description: Annual traveling fashion show created in Chicago in 1958 by Eunice Walker Johnson; became the world's largest traveling fashion show, exposing Black audiences — especially in segregated cities — to haute couture while platforming Black models and designers and raising millions for Black charities. Founder of Fashion Fair Cosmetics (1972).

name: House parties and basement parties — ordinary Black nightlife
description: Neighborhood house parties as the base layer of Black Chicago nightlife: DJs in living rooms and basements, social-club dances, union-hall parties; the seedbed from which both steppin' and Chicago house music grew. Contrast with venue-history approaches that focus on clubs.

name: Traveling with the Negro Motorist Green Book — Chicago as destination
description: Black motorists used the Green Book (1936–1966) to find welcoming hotels, restaurants, gas stations, and attractions; Chicago's listings concentrated ~80% in Bronzeville, effectively mapping the everyday Black commercial landscape for travelers.

description: Black-owned soul food restaurants as everyday and Sunday institutions — multi-generational family operations serving smothered pork chops, fried chicken, catfish, greens, mac and cheese — and the practice of eating out after church. Family ownership across generations; resilience through debt and neighborhood change.

description: Watching a Chicago-raised Black headliner host a national network variety show — a brief, landmark TV moment for Black viewers.

name: "Six-hour dollar" circulation claim (DEBUNKED)
description: The widely repeated statistic that a dollar circulates six hours in the Black community traces to a 1996 self-help book that names no study; debunked by Howard University's TruthBeTold and economist William Spriggs as an urban myth. Documented as a Disputed claim to prevent the merge step from treating it as evidence — the leakage campaigns are real; the number is not.

name: A.B. Molar (Moler) Beauty School / Beauty and Culture School
description: Chicago cosmetology school whose 1916 graduation of Marjorie Stewart Joyner broke its color line. A training institution in the Black women's beauty economy: the school supplied the credential that let Black women open independent salons.
era: Operating by 1916; later history not traced

name: Jordan Building
description: A three-story combination store and apartment building commissioned by Black songwriter and music publisher Joseph J. Jordan; the 1985 NPS Black Metropolis nomination identifies it as the start of the series of Black-owned/financed building projects on South State in the 1920s.
notes: Merged into canonical KG 2026-10-03 from ECON-001; source entity IDs: CTL-DR-ECON-001:ECON-037; source research type(s): place.

name: Mary T. Washington Wylie
description: The first Black woman CPA in the United States (1943), Washington trained under Arthur Wilson at Binga State Bank, founded her own South Side firm (1931 or 1939 — disputed), and built Washington, Pittman & McKeever into a training pipeline that made Chicago the national center of Black CPA concentration.

name: Brandon Johnson
description: Chicago's 57th mayor, sworn in on May 15, 2023.
